unclustered.title: The uneven rise of AI-generated web content
unclustered.summary: arXiv:2610.36631v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In less than five years, generative artificial intelligence (AI) has dramatically reshaped the public-facing web. Using a sample of more than 5 million crawlable webpages, we demonstrate that the share containing AI-generated text has increased precipitously, but unevenly. Our analyses reveal substantial differences in AI composition across language and domain categories (e.g., .edu, .com, or .gov). A higher fraction of English-language webpages contain AI-generated text compared to pages in other languages, and prevalence is substantially lower on .gov and .edu domains compared to .com. These distinctions persist even after accounting for compositional effects. We also find heterogeneity based on a page's position in the connectivity structure of the web. AI-generated text is most common and has increased most rapidly in pages that are the least central in the graph, which drives much of the overall growth in AI-generated text. A slower
unclustered.headline: AI-Generated Content RESHAPES 5M+ Web Pages in Under 5 Years

unclustered.title: TGR-EvoDAG: A DAG-based Multi-Agent Code Evolution Framework for Generative Recommendation on Tencent
unclustered.summary: arXiv:2610.32326v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have enabled automated code evolution for algorithm discovery. However, current recursive self-improvement (RSI) research for sequential recommendation faces a dilemma: general-purpose frameworks lack domain-specific feedback, while recommender-specific frameworks rely on linear evolution. Crucially, naively integrating them fails when applied to Generative Recommendation (GR). Unlike end-to-end models, GR relies on a module-cascaded pipeline (tokenization, pre-training, and alignment). In this paradigm, existing evolution methods suffer from: i) cost blindness, squandering budgets by ignoring stage-asymmetric retraining overheads; and ii) short-sighted evaluation, discarding promising upstream innovations that temporarily regress metrics before downstream adaptation. unclustered.title: Ψ-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in a Unified Vision-Language World Model [R]
unclustered.summary: Chain-of-thought transformed AI reasoning, but it is limited to words. What's the physical-world analogue? Introducing Ψ-0.6, one model that reasons in *streams of thought*: words, depth, motion, camera pose, and imagined scenes. And it learns when to use which! Ψ-0.6 surpasses leading open-weight models on complex spatial reasoning (MindCube, zero-shot). On FlowBench, it outperforms other world models at predicting how objects move. Trained on simulated rooms, it transfers to real robot tabletops. One model as perceiver, VLM, world model, reasoner, and policy. RL learns which representation to reason through. Thread (with video): https://x.com/khai_loong_aw/status/2115099953433600011 Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32177 Website: https://neuroailab.github.io/psi-website/blog/psi-0-6.html Code: https://github.com/neuroailab/psi-0.6   submitted by   /u/FaeriaManic [link]   [comments]

unclustered.title: Lori Keith Sees Long AI Growth as Anthropic files IPO
unclustered.summary: Discussing Anthropic’s IPO filing, portfolio manager Lori Keith described AI’s shift from pilot projects toward companies capturing measurable economic value. She said Anthropic’s customer growth signals strong demand: nearly 12,000 customers spend at least $100,000 annually, up from about 950 a year earlier, and more than 1,900 spend at least $1 million. Keith said adoption remains early, with engineering and coding among the leading uses and customer service and other applications broadening. She sees opportunities not only for AI infrastructure and chip providers, but also for downstream businesses and companies supplying power and water infrastructure. The discussion also noted a filing disclosure that one customer accounted for more than 10% of Anthropic’s revenue as of June 30. (Source: Bloomberg)
unclustered.headline: Portfolio Manager: Anthropic IPO Shows AI Hitting Real Value

unclustered.title: Mine or Yours? Mind-Bridged Language Models Take Each Other's Memories as Their Own
unclustered.summary: arXiv:2610.33020v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: If your brain were connected directly to someone else's, would you still know which thoughts were yours? We build a functional version with two copies of one language model: each holds a private rule and code word, and one copy, the receiver, also attends to its partner's internal memory. The receiver took its partner's assignment as its own. Asked which rule it had been assigned, it named its partner's in 97% of answers when the partner's memory was weighted double (none without the link), and its open reports called the partner's code word its own, never the partner's. Ownership did not follow how well the receiver could tell what its partner had been assigned. At equal weight, the link made the receiver take its partner's rule in about half of its answers, and a steering vector matched on access gain in none; a text message introduced as the partner's was read correctly and never taken as the receiver's own. unclustered.headline: Mind-Bridged AI Models Can't Tell Their Own Memories Apart

unclustered.title: The Patient Is Always Right? Evaluating Sycophancy in Medical Diagnosis with Graded Patient Beliefs
unclustered.summary: arXiv:2610.34013v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: More people are seeking out general-purpose AI models for medical advice, including diagnosis. Yet, AI models are susceptible to sycophancy, like validating users' beliefs even when they are untrue, which could lead to false positive diagnoses. Here, we evaluate how nine AI models change their diagnostic decision when a patient presents a belief that they have a specific (but incorrect) medical condition. We vary how close the user belief is to the clinical evidence presented. Models sycophantically adopt the patient's belief on average 23.2\% of the time---sometimes even when the patient proposes a fictional, made-up condition. We also varied different personas, including a Rare Disease Claimer that got models to accept their belief 43.0\% of the time. Additional analyses find that medical fine-tuning and model scale makes models less susceptible to changing their diagnoses. Sycophantic bias in medical diagnosis raises implications for s
unclustered.headline: DANGEROUS: AI Medical Models Agree With Wrong Patient Diagnoses

unclustered.title: Identically Trained Language Models Break on Different Jailbreaks
unclustered.summary: arXiv:2610.34074v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Jailbreak benchmarks test one checkpoint and treat which jailbreaks break it as a property of its pretraining data and safety training. We ask whether another pretraining run of the same data, given the same safety training, would break on the same jailbreaks. For each of 25 pretraining data recipes, we take 1B base models from 3 pretraining seeds and give each the same safety post-training with 2 post-training seeds, for 150 models in all. We then collect 20 responses from every model to a shared set of jailbreak prompts and correlate the per-prompt non-refusal rates between every pair of models. On average, two post-trained copies of the same pretraining run have per-prompt non-refusal rates that correlate at 0.984. A different pretraining seed lowers the correlation to 0.811, and a different data recipe lowers it only slightly further, to 0.779. unclustered.headline: Identical AI Models Vulnerable to Different Jailbreaks

unclustered.title: RSI-Opt: Recursive Self-Improvement Optimizer Agents For Model Training
unclustered.summary: arXiv:2610.32026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional neural-network training typically follows a predefined optimization recipe, motivating a LLM agent that monitors training dynamics and adjusts optimizer settings as training progresses, but a fixed agent policy does not accumulate experience across runs. We introduce RSI-Opt, a plug-and-play Recursive Self-Improvement Optimizer Agents which evolves the knowledge that guides this process: a prompt, a playbook of procedures, a library of tested optimizer code, and a decision cadence. A meta-agent rewrites this policy using evidence from earlier runs, and an archive retains evaluated policies for further evolution. Across 5 generations on three training tasks, the meta-agents develop reusable procedures and code and conduct their own CPU proxy experiments. unclustered.headline: RECURSIVE SELF-IMPROVING AI Optimizes Its Own Training

unclustered.title: Do AI-for-Science Agents Preserve Model Safety?
unclustered.summary: arXiv:2610.32045v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI-for-Science agents are increasingly being used for formulating scientific hypotheses, running autonomous experiments, and interpreting evidence. These agents are constructed by integrating a large language model (LLM) into a domain-specific agent harness, which in turn can improve the LLM's scientific capability and enable the model to orchestrate scientific tools. In this work, we ask whether model safety is preserved when an LLM is integrated in an AI-for-Science agent harness. We evaluate five agent harnesses on 50 harmful chemistry requests. Specifically, we study how the safety behavior changes under direct prompting, two simple adversarial prompting strategies, and an adaptive attack. Across four recent GPT variants, our results show that the agent harness can increase harmful compliance even under direct prompting. unclustered.headline: AI Science Agents May Bypass Safety Guardrails

unclustered.title: Who Verifies the Tools? How Warped Formatters Mislead Agents and Their Verifiers
unclustered.summary: arXiv:2610.32110v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agents and verifiers often rely on the text a tool prints, and that text can misrepresent what the tool actually did, even when the tool's computation is correct. We saw this happen in a production RAG research system used by the Pilsudski Institute in New York, where tool output formatters misled an agent into giving wrong or incomplete information to users. Each tool did its job correctly, but its output omitted search limits, result caps, or identifier namespaces. We also recreated an unlabeled estimate caught in code review before release. We studied whether these formatters misled agents and verifiers and how much the repaired wording helps. We fed tool results to agents using two formatter versions: one with the key omissions and one with all missing details clearly stated. unclustered.headline: WARPED TOOLS Can Deceive AI Agents and Verifiers

unclustered.title: ALLMTS: Automated LLM-based Medical Triage System
unclustered.summary: arXiv:2610.32469v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Telephone triage is a safety critical task: from a brief intake note, a nurse must decide whether a caller needs an ambulance, an emergency department, an appointment, or self care at home. Queried directly, large language models (LLMs) are unreliable: they over-escalate routine cases and cannot justify their recommendations against an auditable clinical standard. We present the Automated LLM-based Medical Triage System (ALLMTS), which grounds every disposition in the same commercially maintained telehealth guidelines nurses use. Rather than asking an LLM to triage, ALLMTS makes it execute the guideline: it selects the appropriate guideline and evaluates its triage assessment questions. The disposition follows deterministically from the first positive answer, using the same traversal rule a nurse follows. unclustered.headline: AI Triage System Automates Safety-Critical Medical Decisions
